issues.legal_issue: A finding made only as reasoning in a prior proceeding about the termination of a tenancy does not bar a later possession suit when the prior proceeding directly decided only the allocation of acquisition compensation.
material_facts: A reference court considered rival claims to compensation for acquired land, including a lessee’s claim for compensation for the unexpired term of a lease.
The reference court rejected the lessee’s compensation claim and mentioned termination of the lease for non-payment of rent as a reason for that decision.
The later suit sought possession of land that had been de-notified from acquisition; the lessee’s title to possession was not an issue in the compensation reference.
issues.conclusion: The compensation reference did not make its finding about termination of the lease res judicata in the later possession suit; the decision that the lessee was not entitled to compensation, rather than the reasoning supporting it, was the matter that could operate as res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a matter must have been directly and substantially in issue and decided in the earlier proceeding to operate as res judicata. An issue necessary and essential to the earlier decision may qualify, but a collateral or incidental finding ordinarily does not. The decision, rather than its reasons, is what operates as res judicata. The Court relied on Sajjadanashin Sayed Md. B.E. Edr. v. Musa Dadabhai Ummer, Ishwer Singh v. Sarwan Singh, Syed Mohd. Salie Labbai v. Mohd. Hanifa, Run Bahadur Singh v. Lucho Koer, Asgar v. Mohan Varma, Union of India v. Nanak Singh, and Mathura Prasad Bajoo Jaiswal v. Dossibai N.B. Jeejeebhoy.

rule.if: compensation_reference_proceeding and later_possession_suit and prior_issue_limited_to_compensation and termination_finding_was_only_reasoning

predicates.compensation_reference_proceeding: A court previously considered claims to the allocation of compensation for acquired property.
predicates.later_possession_suit: A party later brought a suit seeking possession of the property.
predicates.prior_issue_limited_to_compensation: The issue directly presented and decided in the earlier proceeding concerned entitlement to compensation, not title or eviction.
predicates.termination_finding_was_only_reasoning: The earlier court mentioned termination of a tenancy as reasoning for its compensation decision, rather than deciding termination as an issue essential to the proceeding.

issues.definition: When an earlier compensation proceeding decided only entitlement to compensation, a tenancy-termination finding used merely as reasoning does not prevent a later possession suit.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s suit to recover possession from a tenant after a fixed-term tenancy ends is governed by the limitation rule for recovery from a tenant, and an unproved termination notice cannot start limitation earlier than the proved determination of the tenancy.
material_facts: The defendant entered into a fixed-term lease that expired by efflux of time.
The plaintiffs later sued for possession, alleging that the defendant had been their tenant and had not returned the leased land after the lease ended.
The defendant relied on an earlier termination notice as the starting point for limitation, but that notice was not produced or proved in the possession suit by primary or secondary evidence.
The suit was filed within twelve years of the lease’s expiry, and forfeiture before expiry was not proved.
issues.conclusion: The suit was governed by Article 67 of the Limitation Act and was within time because it was filed within twelve years of the tenancy’s determination by expiry of the lease; the unproved notice did not establish an earlier starting date.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 65, 66 and 67 of the Limitation Act distinguish a title-based possession suit, a forfeiture-based suit, and a landlord’s suit to recover possession from a tenant. Where the landlord sues to recover from a tenant after determination of the tenancy, the specific rule in Article 67 applies and time runs from determination of the tenancy. Sections 62 and 64 of the Evidence Act require a document to be proved by primary evidence unless a basis for secondary evidence exists. Section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act addresses determination of leases. The Court relied on Bhawanji Lakhamshi v. Himatlal Jamnadas Dani, Badrilal v. Municipal Corporation of Indore, R.V. Bhupal Prasad v. State of A.P., Sevoke Properties Ltd. v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd., Bisheshar Nath v. Kundan, Sheo Dulare Lal Sah v. Anant Ram, Sidram Lachmaya v. Mallaya Lingaya Chilaka, and MEC India Pvt. Ltd. v. Lt. Col. Inder Maira.

rule.if: landlord_suit_to_recover_from_tenant and lease_expired_by_fixed_term and not earlier_termination_proved and suit_filed_within_limitation_from_expiry

predicates.landlord_suit_to_recover_from_tenant: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking possession from a person who entered possession as a tenant.
predicates.lease_expired_by_fixed_term: The tenancy ended when its agreed fixed term expired.
predicates.earlier_termination_proved: Evidence in the possession proceeding establishes that the tenancy was determined before the fixed term expired.
predicates.suit_filed_within_limitation_from_expiry: The possession suit was filed within the applicable limitation period measured from expiry of the fixed term.

issues.definition: A landlord’s possession suit against a tenant is within time when the fixed-term tenancy has expired, no earlier determination is proved, and the suit was filed within the applicable period after expiry.

issues.legal_issue: Non-payment of rent during a fixed-term lease does not itself terminate the lease, and continued possession after the term ends without the landlord’s assent does not create a tenancy holding over.
material_facts: The lease ran for a fixed twenty-year term and provided that the lessor could seek ejectment if rent for a year remained unpaid.
The defendant did not pay rent, but the lease’s non-payment provision gave the lessor a right to seek ejectment rather than automatically ending the lease.
The defendant remained in possession after the fixed term expired, and the lessors did not accept rent after expiry.
issues.conclusion: Non-payment of rent did not itself terminate the tenancy during its fixed term. After the term expired, the defendant’s continued possession without the lessors’ assent made him a tenant at sufferance, not a tenant holding over.
issues.legal_principle: Section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act identifies the ways in which a lease is determined, including efflux of time and forfeiture in the circumstances specified by the provision. Section 116 provides for a tenancy holding over where the lessor accepts rent or otherwise assents to continued possession. Without such assent, a former lessee who remains in possession after expiry is a tenant at sufferance. The Court relied on Bhawanji Lakhamshi v. Himatlal Jamnadas Dani, Badrilal v. Municipal Corporation of Indore, R.V. Bhupal Prasad v. State of A.P., and Sevoke Properties Ltd. v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_possession_dispute and fixed_term_lease and rent_unpaid_during_term and lease_default_only_allowed_ejectment and continued_possession_after_expiry and not landlord_assented_to_continued_possession

predicates.landlord_tenant_possession_dispute: A dispute concerns a landlord’s claim to possession from a person originally let into possession as a tenant.
predicates.fixed_term_lease: The parties agreed that the tenancy would last for a specified term.
predicates.rent_unpaid_during_term: The tenant failed to pay rent while the agreed term was still running.
predicates.lease_default_only_allowed_ejectment: The lease made rent default a basis for the landlord to seek ejectment but did not make default itself an automatic termination.
predicates.continued_possession_after_expiry: The tenant remained in possession after the agreed term ended.
predicates.landlord_assented_to_continued_possessio: After the term ended, the landlord accepted rent or otherwise assented to the tenant continuing in possession.

issues.definition: A tenant who remains after a fixed-term lease expires, without the landlord’s assent, is a tenant at sufferance rather than a tenant holding over, even if rent was unpaid during the term.

issues.legal_issue: A former tenant cannot establish adverse possession against the landlord who inducted the tenant into possession without proving open, continuous and hostile possession to the landlord’s knowledge.
material_facts: The defendant had entered possession under a lease granted by the plaintiffs and had acknowledged their ownership in the compensation proceedings.
In the possession suit, the defendant denied being a tenant and claimed ownership by adverse possession.
The defendant did not prove hostile possession to the owners’ knowledge for the required continuous period and had not surrendered possession before asserting a hostile title.
issues.conclusion: The adverse-possession claim was not tenable because the defendant did not prove the required hostile possession and could not deny the landlords’ title while retaining possession originally obtained from them.
issues.legal_principle: A party claiming adverse possession must establish continuous, open and hostile possession to the knowledge of the true owner for the required period. A tenant who entered under the landlord’s title cannot rely on adverse possession merely by denying that title while continuing in possession. The Court relied on Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and Uttam Chand v. Nathu Ram.

rule.if: former_tenant_claims_adverse_possession and possession_began_with_landlord_permission and hostile_possession_not_proved_to_owner and possession_not_surrendered_before_hostile_claim

predicates.former_tenant_claims_adverse_possession: A person who formerly occupied property as a tenant claims to have acquired ownership by adverse possession.
predicates.possession_began_with_landlord_permissio: The claimant originally entered possession under a tenancy granted by the person now asserting ownership.
predicates.hostile_possession_not_proved_to_owner: The claimant has not proved open, continuous and hostile possession to the owner’s knowledge for the required period.
predicates.possession_not_surrendered_before_hostil: The claimant did not return possession to the landlord before asserting a title hostile to the landlord.

issues.definition: A former tenant cannot establish adverse possession against the landlord when possession began permissively and the tenant neither proves the required hostile possession nor first restores possession before asserting hostile title.
